title: A well-made head
hook: better a well-made head than a well-filled one (Essays 1.26)

segments.voice: Yesterday, just custom: the woman who carried a calf until it was an ox. Your line was just custom. What normal thing turned out to be a choice? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

A trivia night at a bar. One team has a member who knows every capital, every element, every year a war ended. They win. Later that week, the same person is asked to help a friend decide whether to take a job in another city, and has nothing to offer but more facts. A head can be very full and still not very useful. Montaigne wrote a long essay on how to raise a child, and in it he draws exactly this line, in one plain phrase.
screen: `A WINNING TRIVIA TEAM.` → `NO HELP WITH A REAL CHOICE.` → `FULL, BUT NOT USEFUL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. When choosing a tutor for a child, Montaigne says, look for one with a well-made head rather than a well-filled one. Both would be good, he allows, but character and understanding matter more than learning. Second, the funnel. Teachers, he complains, keep shouting into children's ears as if pouring into a funnel, and the child's only job is to repeat what was said. He wants the opposite: let the student taste things, choose, and tell them apart. Sometimes the tutor opens the way. Sometimes he lets the student open it. And he puts it bluntly: knowing something by heart is not knowing it. Third, the bees. Bees go from flower to flower taking what they like, Montaigne says, but afterward the honey they make is all their own. It's no longer thyme or marjoram. A student should do the same with what they borrow from books: turn it into their own judgment. Fourth, the test. How do you know someone has learned? Not by what they can recite. By how they live. Montaigne has a homely picture for it: if food comes back up just as it went down, it was never digested. Learning that comes out word for word, the same way, hasn't been taken in. Away from the classroom, a well-made head can belong to the friend who knows few capitals but asks the one question that helps you decide.
screen: `WELL MADE, NOT WELL FILLED.` · `NOT A FUNNEL.` · `BEES MAKE THEIR OWN HONEY.` · `PROOF IS IN HOW YOU LIVE.` · then, large: `WELL MADE, NOT FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: understand one thing well. Sit and let the breath settle. Then pick one idea from these days on the path that you could recite but maybe couldn't explain. Water. The runaway horse. Custom. Different roads. Choose one. Now, in your head, put it in your own words, as if you were telling a twelve-year-old at the kitchen table. No quoting. If it falls apart, that's useful too. Try again, plainer. The bell holds the time.
A well-made head. Montaigne's picture of a good mind: not stuffed with facts, but able to judge, like bees turning flowers into honey of their own. Today's word.
Your line: well made, not full. Today, instead of learning one more fact, explain one thing you already know to someone, in your own words. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay on the education of children take its line about a well-made head as a case for teaching judgment over memorization.

myth: Montaigne says knowing by heart is knowing
he says the opposite: knowing something by heart is not knowing it.
Montaigne says the bees' honey is no longer thyme or marjoram
they take from many flowers, but the honey is all theirs. so with what a student borrows.
Montaigne wants the tutor to fill the child with as many facts as possible
he wants a tutor with a well-made head, who lets the child taste, choose and judge.

fork.setup: you're choosing a tutor for a child. one has read everything. the other has fewer books but sound judgment. what does Montaigne advise?
options: the one with sound judgment, a well-made head.
no tutor; let the child teach himself.
fork.reveal: both would be good, he allows, but he'd rather a well-made head than a well-filled one: understanding and character before learning.

original.note: French: a well-made head, from Montaigne's line on choosing a tutor.

trapdoor: what you thought: a well-made head means being smart.
what it means: a mind that can judge and use what it knows, rather than one stuffed with facts.
what a scholar hears: Montaigne's bees turn borrowed flowers into honey of their own, his picture of how reading should become judgment.

sources.ref: Essays 1.26, Of the education of children (a tutor with a well-made rather than well-filled head; teachers pouring as into a funnel; let the student taste, choose and discern; to know by heart is not to know; the bees and their honey; undigested food as a sign of learning not taken in)

notes: Essays 1.26 (path numbering; 1.25 in some English editions) paraphrased throughout. Montaigne's French: 'plutôt la tête bien faite que bien pleine'; 'savoir par cœur n'est pas savoir'. Confirm.
The essay is addressed to a noblewoman about her expected child; the script leaves out the name.
Montaigne writes of the pupil as a boy; the script uses 'the student' and 'the child' and keeps 'teach himself' only in a fork option.
Editor: varied the stock 'on an ordinary Tuesday' turn and softened the closing image so it doesn't overstate; no factual changes needed.
